item.title: Meet Metakse Ghambaryan: The Armenia Stock Exchange’s Crypto Lead Joins the FIO Board
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
A jump from iGaming into running a crypto exchange, a foundation that teaches a country Web3, and a national stock exchange building a digital asset program. The newest member of the FIO Board works at the one place traditional finance and Web3 actually meet.

Metakse Ghambaryan has been elected to the FIO Board of Directors. She is Crypto Project Lead at the Armenia Stock Exchange, where she runs strategy for the digital asset program, and Director of the Web3 Armenia Foundation.

Her argument for FIO is not about technology. It is about who gets left out when the technology is hard to explain.

From iGaming to the head of a crypto exchange

She arrived in Web3 about six years ago, by an unlikely route.

“I’ve got into this field with an interesting jump from iGaming to Web3 around six years ago. I’ve been promoted to head of a crypto exchange, which was a Chinese crypto exchange but Dubai based.”

What she found there was an information vacuum. Nobody could tell her what Web3 was, so she went and found out, and the search changed how she understood her own profession.

“As a marketer, I got to understand that it is very, very different from what is marketing for crypto and what is marketing overall. This is community building. You have to be 24/7 available for everyone and answer the same question till this day: what is Web3.”

That question, asked over and over by people arriving for the first time, is the thread running through everything she has done since.

Teaching a country

The answer she settled on was education at scale, which is what the Web3 Armenia Foundation does. She is its director.

The work is less glamorous than the word Web3 suggests. It means sitting down with the government, with universities, with crypto exchanges operating physically in the country, and with the international companies arriving in Armenia and needing an introduction to the local network. Alongside that run speaker programs, podcasts, and television appearances, all of them repeating the same patient explanation.

Armenia is further along this road than most people outside the region realize. A country that produces engineers, hosts a Web3 degree program, and is now putting digital assets onto its national exchange is not a minor participant.

The call back

She was working in Uzbekistan, for another crypto exchange, when Armenia called her home.

“I got headhunted back to Armenia to work on our infrastructure.”

The job at the Armenian Stock Exchange is strategy for the digital asset program, and she is clear that the first phase of it looks a lot like the foundation work.

“There is a lot of education here too, because I need my colleagues to understand what is Web3, what is crypto first, and then move to execution part.”

An exchange is a careful institution by design. Bringing one onto blockchain rails is not primarily an engineering problem, and she treats it as a teaching problem first.

Where the two sides meet

That position, between a national exchange and the Web3 community, gives her a clear view of a convergence most people only talk about.

“The next page is fintech getting into tokenization, fintech getting into stablecoins. The borderless idea of Web3 is becoming something that the banks are adopting at the moment.”

She is unsentimental about how differently the two sides think, and unusually direct about what follows from that.

“There is a lot of different mindset between us and the other industry. But as for me, I believe that the future is in the middle. The future is in the dialogue, and the innovation is there. If we keep pushing one side or the other side, we’re going nowhere.”

That is a notable thing for a board member of an onchain naming protocol to say, and it is the reason her appointment matters. The people who will use this technology at scale are not going to arrive through either camp’s front door.

Why FIO

Her test for a project is whether it fills a gap rather than adding another option.

“I’ve always been passionate about working and joining and being a part of projects that are the missing parts of the infrastructure.”

FIO qualifies, by her reading, because it removes the part of crypto that cannot be taught away.

“When you have projects like FIO that bring you this kind of sentence, you just write your handle and all the information is right there. It’s on one infrastructural piece and you have it all. This is very easy for me to get people to understand.”

That last clause is the whole case. Her job is explaining this technology to people who did not ask for it, and a FIO Handle is the rare part that needs no explaining. It is one human-readable name that resolves to a user’s real wallet addresses across supported chains, so a first send looks like typing a name rather than verifying 42 characters.

She makes the same comparison the protocol’s own material makes, arrived at independently.

“When you go to the internet, you don’t care how the domain works with the hosting. You just type in the information you need, you get it.”

And on what she is actually trying to do:

“That’s my job. I want to make Web3 real.”

What this means for holders

Your FIO Handles continue to work. Nothing about this changes what you already hold. Registration continues at app.fio.net, domains at app.fio.net/fio-domain, and FIO remains available across supported partners and exchanges.

Full board election results and vote counts are at fio.net/discover/fio-board-elections.

The long view

What Metakse brings to this board is not a technical specialism. It is a position: she sits inside a traditional financial institution that is moving onchain, and inside a foundation whose job is explaining why that is worth doing. Both roles come down to the same daily task, which is making this comprehensible to people with no reason to be patient with it.

A naming protocol is the same work in a different form.

Metakse is the latest guest on Meet the FIO Board of Directors, the series introducing the people now steering the protocol. She sat down with Wayne Marcel to talk through her route into Web3, what the Armenian Stock Exchange is building, and why the future is in the middle. Watch the episode here.

Her closing words to the community were short:

“Good luck to all of us. Let’s do it.”

item.title: Meet Sipan Vardanyan: The Security Veteran on FIO’s New Board
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
An internet service provider built at thirteen, a bank security career he walked away from, and one of Web3’s busiest offensive security firms. The newest member of the FIO Board of Directors argues that security and usability are not two problems but one.

Sipan Vardanyan has been elected to the FIO Board of Directors. He is the co-founder and chief executive of Hexens, a security firm whose work spans large protocols, centralized exchanges, whole blockchains, and the cryptography underneath them. Before that he spent his career defending banks, ending as a chief information security officer.

He arrives with a blunt argument. The two things holding this industry back are security and usability, and of the two, usability may be the worse problem.

An internet provider at thirteen, then the bank

He started young. At thirteen he built one of the first high-speed internet service providers in his hometown in Armenia, in the window right after people lost their patience with dial-up connections.

Banking came next, five or six years across several institutions, first in senior IT and then as chief information security officer. He is direct about how that chapter ended.

“The day I left, I promised myself I’m not going to work in a bank a single day more.”

What pulled him out was offensive security, the practice of attacking a system yourself to find out how it fails before somebody else does. He and Vahe Karapetyan, a friend who would go on to co-found Hexens with him, had become convinced that decentralized finance, mostly on Ethereum at the time, was where that work was heading.

Hexens, and the exploits nobody has found yet

Hexens came out of that conviction, founded by the two of them. He describes it as a full-spectrum offensive security boutique, working with the largest protocols in the space, with centralized exchanges, with entire blockchains, and on cryptographic security. The firm has just launched Glider Monitor, which Hexens describes as the first continuous threat exposure management system built for Web3.

His read on the current wave of exploits is the part worth sitting with.

“People falsely think that if something is not getting hacked right now, it’s basically safe. It’s just not being targeted yet.”

The tooling has changed, and not in defenders’ favor.

“AI just lowers the entry bar for anybody who wants to do anything. Also black hat stuff. So it’s easier than ever right now to hack stuff.”

That is a security professional describing an environment where old code gets re-examined by cheaper and faster attackers. Bugs that sat untouched for years are now worth someone’s afternoon.

Why FIO

He came to FIO through a friend, then put his own team on researching it before saying yes.

“There is basically so much upside and so much potential in this, because we see how institutional money is already finding its own way into the Web3.”

What that research turned up was a market shifting underneath the protocol.

“Web3 is not Web3 anymore. It’s kind of merging with the traditional finance. I believe we’re going to end up somewhere in Web 2.5, maybe just a tiny bit higher.”

He has been in crypto for over a decade, long enough to recognize the shape of what follows institutional money. Retail interest comes behind it, and the people arriving in that wave have no patience for the current experience. That, in his reading, is FIO’s opening, if the protocol is positioned and executed well.

Security and usability are the same problem

Start with the security half, which is his profession.

“We’re so dependent on a single line of code. A single line of code that is written wrong can lead to hundreds of millions of dollars being stolen.”

Then the turn, and it is not the one you would expect from a career security specialist.

“The usual people, they don’t want to understand how the blockchain works. They don’t want to actually do the research and understand which blockchain is faster or which one is better. Is it easy to use? Is it intuitive? Is it doing what I wanted to do? That’s the main questions that we need to answer. And technology should lie on the back end. You don’t need to see that.”

That is FIO’s design premise, stated by someone who came to it from the outside. A FIO Handle is one human-readable name that resolves to a user’s real wallet addresses across supported chains. The mapping lives onchain, the sender types a name instead of a long string of characters, and the complexity stays where it belongs, underneath.

The reputation problem

The harder inheritance is trust. His account of it is unsentimental: people lost money to pump and dumps, to scam coins, to honeypots, and the specific mechanism stopped mattering to them a long time ago.

“What you’re going to say to a person who lost all his life savings on some random stuff he didn’t fully and completely understand? It’s really, really hard to change that. And that’s going to be one of the goals that we as a community have to try solving.”

Naming this as board-level work, rather than a marketing problem, is a useful signal about how he intends to operate.

What he came to do

Asked for closing words to the FIO community, he offered a warning about how controversial it might sound, then said this.

“I kind of don’t even care about any tokens out there. What I care about is creating value. If I can help you guys to create more value for the end users, if I can be helpful at that mission, that would be a huge goal for me.”

And on how growth actually arrives.

“Compounding value for the community is the number one driver for the growth. It’s not fake marketing. It’s not the advertisement budget that you have. It’s: are our users going to love it, are they going to recommend it to their friends. Let’s build something that will last.”

What this means for holders

Your FIO Handles continue to work. Nothing in this transition changes what you already hold. Registration continues at app.fio.net, domains at app.fio.net/fio-domain, and FIO remains available across supported partners and exchanges.

Full board election results and vote counts are at fio.net/discover/fio-board-elections.

The long view

What Sipan brings to the board is a particular kind of skepticism. He has spent his working life looking for the line of code that fails, and he applies the same attention to the gap between what a protocol claims and what a person can actually do with it. Both of those are questions about whether a thing works. He treats them as one job.

Sipan Vardanyan is the second guest on Meet the FIO Board of Directors, the series introducing the people now steering the protocol. He sat down with Wayne Marcel to talk through his path from bank security into Web3, what Hexens sees in the current exploit wave, and why usability is the harder problem. Watch the episode here.

item.title: FIO Handle Registration Live in Atom Wallets
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
Claim your FIO Handle without leaving Atom Wallets

FIO Handle registration is now live, completing the integration we announced earlier this year.

When Atom Wallets integrated FIO Protocol, users could immediately send crypto to any FIO Handle instead of a long blockchain address. We said handle registration was coming soon.

It is here. Atom Wallets users can now create their own FIO Handle directly inside the app, on the @atom domain, and map it to every blockchain address they hold.

One name. Every supported chain. Never copy an address again.

What’s New: Register Your Own Handle In-App

Registration used to mean leaving your wallet. Now it does not.

Inside Atom Wallets you can claim a personalized handle such as yourname@atom, branded in-app as your Atom Handle and powered by FIO Protocol. Once it is yours, it becomes the single address you share with anyone, on any supported chain.

Your handle can map simultaneously to:

  • Your Bitcoin address
  • Your Ethereum address
  • Your Solana address
  • Your TRON address
  • Any other blockchain address you use

Whichever asset someone sends, FIO resolves it to the right address on the right chain. The person sending never sees a 42-character string, and neither do you.

Because FIO Handles are decentralized Web3 identities, your handle is portable, interoperable, and owned by you. It is not an account with Atom Wallets that you lose if you switch apps. It is yours.

Already Live: Sending to Any FIO Handle

Registration joins the capability Atom Wallets shipped first:

  • No more copy-paste anxiety. Enter a handle like alice@atom in the recipient field and the protocol resolves the correct blockchain address behind the scenes.
  • Cross-chain compatibility. Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, or any other supported token routes to the right address on the right chain.
  • Error-free transactions. One mistyped character in an address is irreversible. A handle removes that risk entirely.

Together, the two halves make the loop complete: you can now both receive at your own handle and send to anyone else’s, without an address ever entering the picture.

How to Claim Yours

  1. Open Atom Wallets and go to the Atom Handle section.
  2. Choose the handle you want on the @atom domain.
  3. Confirm registration.
  4. Share yourname@atom instead of your addresses.

What is FIO Protocol?

FIO (Foundation for Interwallet Operability) Protocol replaces complex public addresses with easy-to-remember, human-readable handles. Think of it as the username for your entire crypto portfolio, across every supported blockchain.

Instead of sharing an address like 0xAb5801a7D398351b8bE11C439e05C5B3259aeC9B, you share yourname@atom.

About Atom Wallets

Atom Wallets is a next-generation, non-custodial cryptocurrency wallet platform that lets users manage and self-custody their digital assets.

The platform uses industry-standard cryptographic practices and local key storage so that private keys remain on the user’s device, supporting a user-controlled, self-custody model intended to minimize reliance on third parties. Privacy-focused design is emphasized, with minimal personal data collection required.

Atom Wallets supports 9+ blockchains including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, BNB Chain, and XRP. Key features include sending and receiving crypto, token swaps via integrated DEX, staking, crypto-to-fiat conversion to local bank accounts, paying network fees in USDT without holding TRX, and a built-in portfolio tracker.

Available on Google Play, App Store and at atomwallets.com.

About FIO Protocol

FIO, the Foundation for Interwallet Operability, is a decentralized consortium supporting the development, integration, and promotion of the FIO Protocol. Built on FIO Chain, a dPoS blockchain, it is an open-source, decentralized usability layer that works across all blockchains. FIO Protocol uses human-readable Handles to replace the complexity, risk, and inconvenience of blockchain-based transactions. The FIO Token ($FIO) powers transactions and incentivizes network participants.

Follow us and join the conversation on X.

item.title: Meet Artyom Harutyunyan: Co-Founder and Board Director of FIO’s Next Chapter
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
A cryptography doctorate, a Web3-only engineering firm, and the world’s only Web3 bachelor’s degree program. Here is the person now driving FIO’s technical and strategic direction.

When FIO token holders went to vote on August 16, 2026, they were not just filling nine board seats. They were confirming a handoff.

Artyom Harutyunyan was elected to the FIO Board of Directors, and he arrives as a co-founder of the new stewardship now carrying the protocol forward, alongside Vardan Khachatryan on legal and regulatory and Narek Gevorgyan on product and growth. The three are co-founders of the Web3 Armenia Foundation, and together they anchor FIO’s next phase. Artyom leads the technical and strategic direction.

The mission has not changed. FIO still exists to make crypto usable through human-readable names instead of long, error-prone wallet addresses. What has changed is who is building it and how far they intend to take it.

A builder since the early Ethereum days

Artyom holds a doctoral degree in cryptography and has worked in this field since Ethereum’s earliest days. He founded Blockstars Technology, an outsourcing firm built exclusively for Web3 at a time when most engineering shops hedged by keeping one foot in traditional software.

He has been through more than one cycle, and his read on what survives them is blunt.

“Coin is nothing, technology is everything. FIO still has the technology, which keeps growing.”

That is not a slogan. It is the reason the handoff makes sense. FIO’s protocol work continued through a downturn that emptied out much of the field, and the people stepping in are the kind who evaluate a project by its codebase rather than its chart.

Building the talent pipeline in Armenia

Artyom’s other long-running project is educational. The Web3 Armenia Foundation, the privately funded nonprofit he co-founded, works on three fronts at once: education, regulatory engagement, and direct support for startups. The practical effect is to help people avoid scams and to give local founders somewhere to turn.

The centerpiece is a university bachelor’s degree program in Web3, which Artyom describes as the only one of its kind in the world. Specialists from across the international industry teach into it, so students work through the history of the technology, the cryptography underneath it, and the applied question of how these systems can serve people the banking system has left behind.

“We have sixty students every year. Exams are harsh, but the students are very potent. We hire them by the third grade.”

Sixty engineers a year is not a rounding error in a field this size. It is one of the few places on earth producing developers who arrive already fluent in this stack, and that pipeline now sits directly behind FIO.

The case for FIO

Artyom’s argument for the protocol is about market structure, not sentiment. He came to the board having concluded that FIO’s market difficulties and FIO’s actual assets were two different things. The technology, the existing integrations, and the user base were all still there.

Wallets, chains, and applications have each built their own naming conventions. Most competitors solve it for one chain. What has never emerged, despite several serious attempts, is a single layer that works across all of them, and several projects aimed at that problem have since pivoted away from Web3 entirely. The gap they left is still wide open.

“There is no global cross-chain naming system, which is like a good niche. FIO has the full potential of becoming the industry’s standard.”

Standards tend to go to whoever is still building when the field thins out. The field has thinned considerably.

FIO 2.0 and the agentic era

The technical expression of that thesis is FIO 2.0. FIO was built on EOS, and the migration to an EVM-compatible chain opens the protocol to a far larger ecosystem of wallets, apps, and developers, while handling more transaction volume and keeping the features holders already depend on.

Four workstreams sit behind it:

Chain migration. Moving off the EOS-based system to EVM compatibility, for accessibility and throughput.

Swap-on-send. Send an asset, and it arrives in the format the recipient actually wants, whichever chain they are on. The bridging happens underneath, where the user does not have to think about it.

Privacy. Methods for obscuring the endpoints of a transaction.

Agent identity. A naming system for AI agents, so an agent keeps a consistent address even when the wallet address underneath it changes.

“FIO made crypto usable through readable names. FIO 2.0 aims higher: private transactions, seamless transfers across any chain, and an identity layer built for AI agents that transact on your behalf. Same mission, ready for what’s next.”
Artyom Harutyunyan

That last one is worth sitting with. As AI agents begin transacting on people’s behalf, the question of who or what an address belongs to stops being a convenience problem and becomes an infrastructure problem. An agent that has to re-learn an address every time the underlying wallet rotates is an agent that will eventually send funds to the wrong place. A stable, readable, verifiable name solves that, and FIO has been building that layer since before there was a name for the use case.

What this means for holders

Your FIO Handles continue to work. This transition expands what is possible rather than replacing what you have. Registration continues at app.fio.net, domains at app.fio.net/fio-domain, and FIO remains available across supported partners and exchanges.

Full board election results and vote counts are at fio.net/discover/fio-board-elections.

The long view

What comes through most clearly in conversation with Artyom is that he treats education and infrastructure as one project. You cannot build a usable Web3 on a public that does not understand it, and you cannot teach people to build on a foundation that does not work. He has been working both ends for years, and now he is doing it with FIO.

Artyom is the first guest on Meet the FIO Board of Directors, a new series introducing the people the community elected. He sat down with Wayne Marcel to talk through his path into Web3, the Armenia program, and where cross-chain naming goes next. Watch episode one here.

item.title: FIO’s Next Chapter: New Stewardship, a New Chain, and What It Means for You
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
A community update

The last stretch has been one of the most significant in FIO’s history — not because the mission changed, but because the people and the technology carrying it forward are stepping into a new era. If you’ve held a FIO Handle or followed the protocol for a while, here’s a clear, no-spin look at what’s happening and what it means for you.

New stewardship

FIO’s next phase is being led by a new team anchored around the Web3 Armenia Foundation, with co-founders Artyom Harutyunyan, Vardan Khachatryan, and Narek Gevorgyan driving the technical, legal, and product direction respectively.

This is a deliberate handoff into a group that’s committed to building FIO for the long term. The vision that made FIO matter in the first place -making crypto usable through human-readable names instead of long, error-prone wallet addresses- stays exactly the same. What’s new is the momentum behind it.

The new board is elected

The community has spoken. FIO’s Board of Directors is made up of up to nine members, elected directly by FIO token holders- one FIO token equals one vote. In the elections held August 16, 2026, token holders voted in the directors below to steward FIO’s next chapter, bringing together the team driving FIO forward alongside longtime community members, block producers, and builders from across the ecosystem.

Your newly elected directors:

  • Ross Dold — a longtime FIO community member and infrastructure operator (Eosphere), supporting the protocol since launch.
  • Eugene Luzgin — co-founder of Crypto Tribe (formerly EOS Tribe) and an active FIO Chain block producer and validator.
  • Artyom Harutyunyan — leading FIO’s technical and strategic direction (Blockstars / Web3 Armenia).
  • Wayne Marcel — focused on driving the protocol forward and advancing crypto adoption (fio.net).
  • Marina Grigoryan — 5+ years across FIO marketing, communications, community relations, and exchange partnerships.
  • Narek Gevorgyan — product and growth (CoinStats).
  • Vardan Khachatryan — focused on FIO’s legal and regulatory footing.
  • Metakse Ghambaryan — Crypto & Digital Assets project lead (AMX)
  • Sipan Vardanyan — co-founder and CEO of Web3 security firm Hexens, bringing deep security expertise.

Together they represent a clear path forward for token holders, Block Producers, and integrators alike.

Full results and vote counts: https://fio.net/discover/fio-board-elections

FIO 2.0: an EVM-compatible chain

The biggest technical change is FIO 2.0 — a move to an EVM-compatible chain. In plain terms, this opens FIO up to a far larger ecosystem of wallets, apps, and developers, while keeping the features you already rely on. The focus ahead: private transactions, seamless transfers across any chain, and an identity layer built for the agentic era.

“FIO made crypto usable through readable names. FIO 2.0 aims higher: private transactions, seamless transfers across any chain, and an identity layer built for AI agents that transact on your behalf. Same mission, ready for what’s next.”

— Artyom Harutyunyan

What stays the same

  • Your FIO Handles continue to work — this transition is about expanding what’s possible, not replacing what you have.
  • Registration continues at app.fio.net, and domains at app.fio.net/fio-domain.
  • FIO continues to be available across supported partners and exchanges.

What’s next

We’ll keep sharing updates as FIO 2.0 rolls out. The short version: new stewardship, a bigger technical foundation, and a governance model that puts the community at the center. Same mission, more ways to win.

About FIO:

FIO Protocol uses human-readable Handles to replace the complexity, risk, and inconvenience associated with blockchain-based transactions. Users register FIO Domains (like @wallet or @edge) and create FIO Handles (like alice@wallet) on those domains. These web3 domains and handles can map to blockchain addresses across every chain. Fueling the ecosystem utilization is the FIO Token ($FIO), which powers transactions and incentivizes network participants.

item.title: A New Chapter for FIO: The Protocol Transitions to Community Stewardship
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
After years of building, integrating, educating, and advocating, the FIO Foundation is formally transitioning full stewardship of the FIO Protocol from the Foundation to the FIO community.

From day one, the FIO Foundation was chartered not to run, manage, or control the protocol, but to facilitate its growth until the ecosystem could stand on its own. That time has arrived. The Foundation is stepping back so that the community, the Block Producers, the integrators, the developers, and the token holders can step forward as the protocol’s permanent stewards.

What this means:

  • FIO Chain: The chain is a battle-tested fully decentralized, public Delegated Proof of Stake network operated by independent Block Producers around the world. It does not depend on the Foundation to produce blocks, validate transactions, or resolve FIO Handles.
  • Your FIO Handles, Domains, and Tokens: Registrations, renewals, transfers, requests, mappings, and all protocol functionality continue to operate exactly as they do today.
  • The protocol: The FIO protocol keeps evolving. FIO Improvement Proposals (FIPs), the Bug Bounty Program, and the open-source repositories on GitHub remain the way changes get proposed, reviewed, and shipped.
  • Governance: The on-chain machinery that makes FIO decentralized is not going anywhere. Token holders vote for Block Producers. Block Producers set fees and approve smart contract changes by supermajority. If you hold FIO tokens, get involved in the governance of the chain.

What is changing is that the Foundation itself, as a Cayman non-profit entity with a Board, Steering Committee, and Worker Proposal structure, will be sunsetting its legal entity operations. The work that has historically sat inside that structure will transition to community-led efforts, and any remaining treasury assets will be allocated toward outstanding obligations and dissolution costs.

Why This, and Why Now

Foundations, by design, are scaffolding. They are supposed to eventually come down. Several converging realities have brought us to this decision:

The protocol has matured. FIO Handles, Domains, Requests, Data, NFT signatures, and handle mapping are live, documented, SDK-supported, and integrated across dozens of wallets and exchanges. The core product is open source, and it is battle-tested on mainnet. Block Producers already run infrastructure and secure the chain. Independent developers already submit FIPs and maintain SDKs. Integrators already market and onboard users. Much of what the Foundation funds is work the community is already doing.

Foundation Reserves have been depleted. The 181,253,654 FIO Tokens that were reserved at Mainnet launch to seed Foundation operations, minted at 150,000 per day, ran out in July 2023. Since then, the Foundation has operated on transaction fees, TPID rewards, and reserves built up during earlier years. Following Binance’s recent delisting of the FIO Token, that treasury has now reached a point where continuing to support an already decentralized protocol is no longer the most sustainable structure for this ecosystem.

We recognize this is a significant transition, and we have chosen to approach it deliberately. After careful deliberation, the Board and Steering Committee concluded that the right path is to transition in an orderly, well-supported way. We believe the healthiest long-term outcome for FIO is a protocol that belongs entirely, operationally and philosophically, to the people who use it and build on it.

How Stewardship Transitions to the Community

Elements of the transition plan are already in motion. Some will happen over the coming months.

Block Producers become the primary operational backbone

The 21 active and 21 standby Block Producers already secure the chain, validate every transaction, approve smart contract changes by 2/3 + 1 supermajority, and set fees through continuous median submission. Going forward, Block Producers will also take the lead on:

  • Coordinating protocol upgrades and emergency response
  • Maintaining the core chain software and contract repositories
  • Approving and shepherding FIPs through review to deployment
  • Publishing status updates and health metrics for the network
  • Administering the Bridge Custodian set that operates the ETH, Polygon and Base bridges

If you are not already voting for Block Producers or proxying your FIO Tokens to someone who is, now is the moment to do so. Block Producer elections are the most direct lever token holders have to shape who operates and evolves the protocol. Every FIO Token is a vote.

The FIP process remains the canonical way changes happen

Nothing about FIO Improvement Proposals changes structurally. Anyone can still open a FIP in the fioprotocol/fips repository on GitHub. Community review still happens in the open. Block Producer supermajority still governs contract deployment. What changes is that the Foundation will no longer be the default sponsor, impact-statement author, or funder for new FIPs. That role moves to the community: Block Producers, integrators, and independent contributors who care enough about an improvement to shepherd it.

Ongoing revenue streams

The protocol’s economic model does not depend on the Foundation to keep running. Block Producers continue to receive 60% of every fee collected. Stakers continue to receive 25%. Integrators continue to receive 10% of fees via TPID (currently boosted to 50% via New User Bounties for qualifying integrators) and 11% of staking rewards when their users unstake. These flows are enshrined in the chain itself. They do not switch off.

The 5% of fees historically paid to the Foundation will be addressed as part of the transition. Options on the table include redirecting this share to Block Producers, to a community-controlled treasury, to stakers, or to a combination, subject to a FIP and Block Producer approval. We will not make this decision unilaterally. The community will.

Websites, documentation, and infrastructure

fio.net, dev.fio.net, the FIO Dashboard, and other Foundation-operated properties will transition to community maintainers where there is willingness and capacity to take them over, or will be archived in a way that preserves history and keeps the ecosystem documented. Source code and documentation are already open source.

Partnerships and integrations

Integrators who have active partnerships, co-marketing commitments, or in-flight integration work with the Foundation will be contacted directly. We will do our best to hand off relationships gracefully, to community members or Block Producer teams where appropriate.

A Word of Thanks

We extend our sincere thanks to every integration partner, Block Producer, token holder, community member, and contributor who believed in the mission of making blockchain usable for everyone. Special thanks to our early supporters, including Binance Labs, who led the Foundation’s Series A funding.

The code is open-sourced. The chain is running. The community that built it moves forward. The FIO Protocol endures.

— The FIO Foundation

item.title: Send Crypto the Easy Way: FIO’s Web3 Domains Comes to Atom Wallets
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
Seamless, human-readable crypto transfers arrive on one of the fastest-growing multi-chain wallets

We’re thrilled to announce that Atom Wallets has integrated FIO Protocol, bringing human-readable FIO Handles to its global community of crypto users. This partnership makes sending cryptocurrency as simple as sharing a username, removing the need to copy and paste long, error-prone blockchain addresses.

Atom Wallets users can now send crypto to any FIO Handle directly within the app. And soon, they’ll be able to register their own FIO Handle without ever leaving the wallet.

What is FIO Protocol?

FIO (Foundation for Interwallet Operability) Protocol transforms the way you interact with blockchain technology by replacing complex public addresses with easy-to-remember, human-readable handles. Think of it as the “username” for your entire crypto portfolio across all blockchains.

Instead of sharing addresses like 0xAb5801a7D398351b8bE11C439e05C5B3259aeC9B, you can simply use your FIO Handle like yourname@wallet to receive crypto on any blockchain.

What’s Live Now: FIO Send

Atom Wallets has integrated FIO Send, enabling users to send any supported cryptocurrency to a FIO Handle instead of a traditional blockchain address. Here’s what that means for you:

  • No more copy-paste anxiety: Enter a simple FIO Handle like alice@domain in the recipient field and the protocol automatically resolves the correct blockchain address behind the scenes
  • Cross-chain compatibility: Whether you’re sending Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, or any other supported token, FIO Handles route your transaction to the right address on the right chain
  • Error-free transactions: Eliminate the risk of sending funds to the wrong address due to a single mistyped character, a mistake that’s irreversible on the blockchain

Sending crypto on Atom Wallets now feels as natural as sending a message to a contact in your phone.

Coming Soon: FIO Handle Registration

We’re excited to share that Atom Wallets will soon integrate FIO Handle registration directly within the app. Users will be able to claim their own personalized FIO Handle and map it to all of their blockchain addresses, creating one universal crypto identity across every chain.

Your FIO Handle can simultaneously map to:

  • Your Bitcoin address
  • Your Ethereum address
  • Your Solana address
  • Your TRON address
  • Any other blockchain addresses you use

One simple, memorable handle for all your crypto. No matter which token someone sends you, FIO knows exactly where to deliver it. And because FIO Handles are decentralized Web3 domains, your identity is portable, interoperable, and fully owned by you.

About Atom Wallets

Atom Wallets is a non-custodial, multi-chain crypto wallet built for secure global payments and everyday crypto use. Originally founded in 2015 as PayAtom, the platform has grown into a comprehensive Web3 wallet supporting thousands of cryptocurrencies across major blockchains including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, BNB Chain, and Polygon.

With true self-custody, instant swaps, crypto-to-fiat conversion, and no KYC required for basic features, Atom Wallets is designed for everyone — from freelancers receiving international payments to traders managing multi-chain portfolios. Available on Google Play and at atomwallets.com.

About FIO Protocol

FIO, the Foundation for Interwallet Operability, is a decentralized consortium that supports the ongoing development, integration, and promotion of the FIO Protocol. The protocol, built on the FIO Chain, a dPoS blockchain, serves as an open-source, decentralized usability layer solution that works across all blockchains. FIO Protocol uses human-readable Handles to replace the complexity, risk, and inconvenience associated with blockchain-based transactions. Fueling the ecosystem utilization is the FIO Token ($FIO), which powers transactions and incentivizes network participants.

item.title: Six Years In: The FIO Protocol Story
item.dc:creator: FIO
item.content:encoded:
Reflecting on What We Built, What We Learned, and What It All Meant

This month marks six years since FIO Protocol went live. In crypto, six years is a lifetime. Projects launch and vanish inside a single market cycle. Narratives shift. Attention moves on. The fact that FIO is still here, still running, still integrated into real products used by real people, is itself a statement worth pausing on.

This anniversary is a chance to look back at what FIO set out to do and what it actually accomplished along the way.

The Problem We Set Out to Solve

In 2019, David Gold and the team at Dapix published the Interwallet Operability Protocol whitepaper. The diagnosis was clear: more than a decade after the Bitcoin whitepaper, the process of actually using crypto remained dangerously unintuitive. Users copied and pasted long hexadecimal addresses and hoped for the best. Transactions were send-only with no standardized way to request payment. One misplaced character could mean permanently lost funds. Nearly one in five crypto users reported failed transactions or lost funds, not from hacks, but from simple human error.

The whitepaper drew a parallel to the early internet: powerful technology that remained inaccessible until a usability layer (DNS) unlocked it for everyone. FIO’s bet was that crypto needed the same thing: a decentralized service layer sitting alongside blockchains, not intermediating their transactions, but making them comprehensible to ordinary people. Human-readable addresses. Payment requests. Transaction metadata. All chain-agnostic, all privacy-preserving, all built on an independent, purpose-built blockchain.

In September 2019, Binance Labs led a $5.7 million Series A funding round to make it happen. By March 2020, FIO Chain was live.

What We Built

Over six years, FIO Protocol delivered on its core technical promise. FIO Handles, human-readable identifiers in the format username@domain, replaced raw public addresses across dozens of wallets, exchanges, and dApps. The FIO Request system brought invoicing to crypto, letting users request payment in a structured, encrypted way that simply didn’t exist before. FIO Data enabled encrypted transaction metadata on any blockchain. FIO Domains gave users ownership over their own namespaces, secured as NFTs by private keys.

Beyond the core protocol, the team shipped several products that made FIO accessible to different audiences. The FIO App (originally the FIO Dashboard) gave users a comprehensive web interface to register and manage handles, stake tokens, vote in governance, sign NFTs, and send FIO Requests, all without needing a third-party wallet. For developers, the Lite SDK stripped integration down to the essentials: a lightweight Typescript library for signing and broadcasting transactions to the FIO Chain, which became the recommended path for most new integrations.

FIO also expanded across chains through its decentralized bridge. Wrapped FIO Tokens on Ethereum opened up trading on Uniswap, while Wrapped FIO Domains on Polygon turned domains into ERC-721 NFTs that could be listed on marketplaces like OpenSea. In January 2026, Wrapped FIO launched on Base, bringing the token into Coinbase’s ecosystem and Base’s DeFi layer.

The Integrations That Defined the Journey

Over the years, FIO was adopted by more than 100 wallets, exchanges, and platforms. A few of those milestones stand out.

In 2022, Opera integrated FIO into its Android browser, offering free @opera crypto handles to millions of users.

In 2024, Ledger accepted FIO’s dedicated app, available through Ledger Live, giving users secure access to staking, governance, and handle management directly from their hardware wallets.

That same year, MetaMask, the largest self-custody wallet in crypto, added FIO Protocol support via their Snap directory, allowing users to send and receive assets to their crypto handles.

Then in early 2025, Trust Wallet made FIO its default handle system, bringing FIO to over 130 million users. Decrypt covered it as a landmark for Web3 usability.

Beyond the headline names, FIO wove itself into a broad ecosystem: Edge Wallet, Bitcoin.com, ChangeNOW, Guarda, CoinStats, ELLIPAL air-gapped wallets, and exchanges including Binance, Kraken, ByBit, and Gate.io.

Each integration represented real engineering work and a real bet by another team that usability mattered enough to build for.

The Community

Some of FIO’s most meaningful work happened at the community level. Over 155 million FIO tokens were staked, a measure of real participation in governance and network security. The FIO Affiliate Program turned community members into active advocates. Handle campaigns under domains like @wallet, @hodl, @moon, and @diamondhands brought personality and identity to what could have been a purely technical product.

FIO’s governance stayed active throughout. Token holders voted in new Board members, most recently this past year. Steering Committee membership shifted over time, bringing in fresh perspectives and different visions for the protocol’s direction. Block Producers voted on protocol changes through supermajority consensus. And community members engaged directly by writing their own FIPs (FIO Improvement Proposals).

The clearest example was FIP-51: a community member proposed that FIO’s Web3 Domains become near-permanent assets with renewal fees reduced to pennies per year. The proposal went through open discussion, technical review, and was approved and implemented by the Block Producers. The result was 50-year domain ownership for roughly $45 total, down from approximately $2,000 under the previous model. That proposal didn’t come from the core team. It came from the community, moved through the governance process, and changed the economics of the protocol.That’s how decentralized governance is supposed to work.

The X Spaces program became another consistent fixture, not just marketing, but genuine conversation. Over the past year alone, the team hosted discussions on everything from NFTs to AI, DePIN infrastructure, privacy, and the role of humor in crypto onboarding. These were substantive, curious conversations that gave FIO a consistent voice in the broader Web3 conversation.

On the Road

For a protocol of its size, FIO showed up everywhere. Over six years, the team represented the project at TOKEN2049, Bitcoin conferences, ETHDenver, NFT.NYC, Permissionless, Consensus, EthCC, Binance Blockchain Week, and more.

Wayne Marcel, Head of Growth, became a familiar face at these events, building connections and making the case for why usability mattered even when the industry’s attention was elsewhere. Marie Grig, Head of Marketing, carried the FIO message from Hong Kong to Bangkok to Paris. Community members showed up too: representing FIO in West Africa and bringing the protocol to India, and hosting Bitcoin Pizza Day celebrations at local events.

What FIO Proved

The core ideas in the 2019 whitepaper were right, and they still are: blockchain addresses should be human-readable, payments should be requestable, metadata should travel with transactions, and usability should be a protocol-level concern rather than an afterthought.

FIO showed that human-readable crypto addresses could work at scale across chains without compromising decentralization or privacy. It brought payment requests to crypto, something every other financial system takes for granted but that blockchain never had. And it showed that a dedicated team and committed community could maintain a decentralized blockchain, ship software continuously, and land integrations with some of the biggest names in the industry.

To Everyone Who Built This

Six years is a long time in any industry, but especially in crypto.

To the developers who wrote and maintained the code. To the block producers who kept the chain running and voted to implement the community’s proposals. To the community members who showed up every week for quizzes, spaces, campaigns, and conversations, and who wrote FIPs that changed how the protocol worked. To the partners who took the time to integrate FIO into their products. To everyone who staked, voted, proposed, and participated: this protocol exists because of you.

Six years. A real protocol. Real technology. Real integrations. A real community that shaped the protocol from within. That is FIO.

With gratitude,

The FIO Team

wFIO launched on Base, and last month we released guides to help users get started with how to buy, trade, and unwrap their tokens. We also hit two major conferences; Consensus HK and ETHDenver, and joined the daGama Global Explorer Quest.

🔗 wFIO on Base

FIO has expanded its multi-chain support by adding wrapped FIO (wFIO) to Base, Coinbase’s Ethereum Layer 2. This new integration joins existing deployments on Ethereum and Polygon. The move to Base is strategic, offering FIO holders advantages such as low-fee Uniswap trading and simple Coinbase on-ramping within the Base ecosystem.

Following the launch of wFIO on Base, we released a series of step-by-step guides to help users navigate the new ecosystem:

  • Buying wFIO via Coinbase: A walkthrough showing how to find the official wrapped FIO contract address, verify it on BaseScan, and purchase wFIO directly on Coinbase using USDC or a bank account.
    🎥Guide
  • Trading wFIO on Uniswap: How to swap USDC for wrapped FIO on Base, including how to verify the correct contract address and avoid fake tokens on DEXs.
    🎥Guide
  • Unwrapping wFIO to Native FIO: A guide for users who’ve purchased wFIO on Base and want to convert it to native FIO inside the FIO App. Connect your wallet, select Base as the source network, choose your FIO Handle, and confirm the unwrap.
    🎥Guide

⚠️ Important reminder: Always search for tokens using the verified contract address, not just the token name, to avoid scams.

Official wFIO Contract Address on Base: 0x134F08385522FDe9dc00725e636343206B4BE97B

This is a great chance to get introduced to our protocol’s offerings: human-readable crypto identity, simplified transactions, and a universal usability layer for all blockchains. The new year kicked off with momentum. January 2026 brought one of FIO’s biggest technical milestones to date: the launch of Wrapped FIO on Base. We also hosted a series of conversations that challenged the Web3 community to think deeper about the new era of the agentic internet, and what decentralization actually means in practice.

🔗 Wrapped FIO Now Live on Base

The headline of the month: wFIO is officially available on Base and trading on Uniswap.

This expansion marks another step in FIO’s multi-chain strategy, bringing the FIO Token to one of Ethereum’s most active Layer 2 networks. Base has captured 46% of all Layer 2 DeFi total value locked, and with Coinbase’s 110 million verified users, wFIO now has access to one of the most vibrant DeFi ecosystems in crypto.

What you can do with wFIO on Base:

  • Trade on Uniswap with minimal fees and near-instant settlement
  • Provide liquidity to the wFIO pool and earn a share of trading fees
  • Access DeFi including lending protocols and yield opportunities as integrations expand

Base joins Ethereum and Polygon in FIO’s growing list of supported networks for wrapped assets.
